Its conventions. A film genre whose plots feature travel, typically sending protagonists away from home to distant or exotic places to fulfill a goal such as a quest or search.

What it asks of an actor. A film reference work treats action and adventure cinema together as a form that foregrounds the body in motion and in combat, with a hero who must show physical endurance. In its swashbuckler strand the hero displays martial skill in extravagant swordplay, and stars such as Fairbanks did much of their own stunt work.

What a self-tape in it asks. A self-tape in it calls for Stage Combat (yours: 48.0 of 90). A night of a play of its kind, or a class scene from one, calls for its own material’s techniques instead.

Why it’s applied, in the research’s words: Tasker’s encyclopedia entry says of the whole form that action and adventure cinema foregrounds the body in motion and in combat, which makes on-screen combat a convention of the genre. It’s one credible source, so the research holds it at medium confidence, not high. Stars doing their own stunts (Fairbanks, Flynn) is a matter for swashbuckler stars, and isn’t what the requirement rests on. What the research says: Action and Adventure Films: "as a form that foregrounds the body in motion and in combat, action and adventure cinema advances a physical (frequently sexualized), imagery of heroism"; "the action or adventure hero is called upon to demonstrate courage, initiative and physical endurance"; the swashbuckler hero is shown "displaying martial skills in extravagant scenes of swordplay"; Flynn’s "athletic performance came to define the romantic male exuberance of the swashbuckler." Douglas Fairbanks: No Stuntman Required: Fairbanks "completed most stunts himself" and secretly did the Robin Hood drawbridge stunt after agreeing to a double. It makes no claim about swashbuckler stars in general. Swordsmen of the Screen: From Douglas Fairbanks to Michael York: Quoted (via Wikipedia, not read directly) as saying that to understand a swashbuckler 'we must look at the art director, costume designer, fencing master, stunt arranger, cinematographer and actor'. The book’s existence and authorship are confirmed by the Wikipedia citation; the quote itself wasn’t seen on a page read directly. (two of its three sources read directly and the remaining one from a search summary, reviewed 2026-10-10; medium confidence). Still uncertain: Tasker treats action and adventure as one form; scholars such as Brian Taves separate historical adventure from action, and some adventure films (travel or exploration stories) have little combat. Only one source says it of the whole genre directly. The Richards quote wasn’t read in the book itself.

How its scenes are played. A reference work treats its hero as a body in motion who must show endurance and carry the quest. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.

Command Of The Frame: Status and threat carried in the body and the look more than the words: the person everyone in the room watches. A self-tape in it is judged more on connection and execution, and calls on your presence and physical expression. Rehearsing on your feet: status is found standing, in how little you need to move.

To study it. Press Study It beside it under Genres on your Player Profile. You’ll watch a film of its kind. Its brief is finished work: you tape it, and it’s judged beat by beat like any taped brief, on what its own material asks.

Its conventions. Drama and film in which conventional plot, characterization and logic are ignored or distorted to convey the irrationality of existence and humanity's isolation in a meaningless world, as in the post-war Theater of the Absurd.

What it asks of an actor. Absurdist drama, Beckett above all, asks actors for exact control of timing, rhythm and timed silence, and in Waiting for Godot for the cross-talk and clown business of vaudeville and music hall.

Why it adds no requirement. What the research found (Comic Timing, Physical Comedy) belongs to Beckett’s plays (Waiting for Godot’s cross-talk and clown business), not to the genre as a whole, so the genre adds no requirement of its own.

What the research says: The study guide, from a search summary: Beckett 'places strong emphasis on the rhythmic qualities of his plays, and like a composer, he is conscious of the importance of precisely timed silence'; his plays put actors in very difficult positions, some unable to speak and others unable to move; one actress says the voice must concentrate on 'timing, rhythm and the musicality of the text'. Wikipedia, from a search summary, says Godot borrows from 'the cross-talk tradition of the vaudeville stage, the burlesque, the music hall, and the movies of Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, Laurel and Hardy', with hat games, dropped trousers and similar business. The Northern Star blog says Godot owes much of its form and rhythm to vaudeville and clown acts. (from a search summary; low confidence). Still uncertain: All of the evidence is Beckett, mostly Godot. Ionesco, Pinter and absurdist film aren’t covered. The study guide’s PDF couldn’t be read as text, so the quotations come from a search engine’s summary of it, not from a direct reading. Nothing found covers 'holding comedy and despair together' as an acting demand in so many words. On review (2026-10-10), evidence that’s all Beckett wasn’t enough to make it a requirement of the whole genre.

How its scenes are played. Beckett’s drama asks for exact control of timing, rhythm and timed silence inside a world whose logic is distorted. This comes from the genre’s research, mostly held with low confidence.

The World’s Own Logic: A world with rules of its own, absurd, dreamlike or satirical, played wholeheartedly by them and never commented on. A self-tape in it is judged more on interpretation and execution, and calls on your imagination and physical expression. The breakdown: the world’s logic has to be found before it can be played as if it were sense.
Comic Rhythm: Setup and payoff: cues picked up, pauses placed, the laugh landing where the timing puts it. A self-tape in it is judged more on responsiveness and execution, and calls on your adaptability and focus. Rehearsing on your feet: timing lives in the exchange and is found by playing it through.

To study it. Press Study It beside it under Genres on your Player Profile. You’ll watch a film of its kind. Its brief is finished work: you tape it, and it’s judged beat by beat like any taped brief, on what its own material asks.
